standard.title: Direct and indirect speech
standard.description: investigate how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech are used
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how different verb types represent doing, feeling, thinking, saying and relating (AC9E3LA07). They have not yet investigated how quoted (direct) and reported (indirect) speech work as distinct grammatical and textual choices.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify direct and indirect speech in texts, explain the grammatical and punctuation differences between them, and describe why a writer might choose one over the other in context.

nodes.label: Direct speech features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify direct speech in a text and describe its key features — quotation marks, saying verb, speaker identification.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify direct speech in a text and name at least two features that mark it as direct speech.
nodes.typical_width: Identify direct speech across narrative and non-narrative texts, naming features including quotation marks, saying verbs, punctuation conventions and speaker identification, and explain what effect hearing the exact words creates.
wider: Compare how direct speech is used in narrative (to reveal character) versus news reporting (to attribute claims) and explain how purpose changes the role of direct speech
Investigate how dialogue in First Nations Australian literary texts uses direct speech to convey voice, community and cultural perspective
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding indirect speech in N2 requires students to know direct speech as the contrast case — indirect features (no quotation marks, tense shift, pronoun change) are defined by how they differ from direct.

response_modes.reason: Direct speech appears across narrative and non-narrative texts with different purposes — students need multiple text contexts to understand it as a deliberate choice, not just 'what people say', before the contrast with indirect speech is meaningful.

success_criteria: Can identify direct speech in a text and name quotation marks and a saying verb as features
Understands that direct speech presents the speaker's exact words

nodes.label: Indirect speech features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify indirect speech in a text and describe its key grammatical features — no quotation marks, tense shift, pronoun change.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify indirect speech in a text and name at least one grammatical feature that distinguishes it from direct speech.
nodes.typical_width: Identify indirect speech across texts and describe its features — reporting verb, subordinate clause with 'that', tense shift, pronoun change — and explain why indirect speech is used to summarise or report rather than quote exactly.
wider: Compare how indirect speech is used differently across text types — reports, recounts, news — and explain why summarising is preferred over quoting in each
Examine how reported speech can change the meaning or emphasis of what was said, and discuss implications for fairness in reporting
nodes.hinge_reason: Explaining the effect of choosing direct versus indirect in N3 requires students to be able to transform between them — students who cannot produce indirect speech accurately cannot evaluate the choice meaningfully.

response_modes.reason: The tense shift and pronoun change in indirect speech are mechanical features students commonly get wrong. Practice across multiple examples is needed before transformation between direct and indirect becomes reliable.

success_criteria: Can identify indirect speech and note that there are no quotation marks
Can explain that indirect speech reports what was said without using the exact words

nodes.label: Choosing between direct and indirect
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why a writer might choose direct speech over indirect speech (or vice versa) in a specific context.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain one reason why a writer uses direct speech in a narrative and one reason indirect speech is used in an informational text.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how direct and indirect speech are used purposefully across narrative and non-narrative texts, explaining the effect of each choice on authenticity, pace, summary and reader engagement.
wider: Rewrite a passage, converting direct to indirect speech and vice versa, and evaluate the effect on tone, pace and authenticity
Compare how direct and indirect speech are used across different media formats — written story, film script, news article — and explain how the medium influences speech choices

response_modes.reason: Students often see direct speech as simply 'what people say' without understanding it as a deliberate stylistic choice. Multiple genre contexts show how writers use speech differently depending on purpose.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The deliberate choice between direct and indirect speech as a stylistic and rhetorical tool is rich territory that connects to persuasion, narrative voice and media literacy.
success_criteria: Can explain why direct speech is used in a narrative (e.g. to show character, create immediacy) and why indirect speech is used in a report (e.g. to summarise efficiently)
Can transform a direct speech sentence into indirect speech correctly
